transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

## What E:09 means

On your Bosch, E:09 is a heating fault. Your model doesn't have a separate exposed element. It uses a "heat pump," which is the main circulation pump with the heating element built into its housing. Stone-cold but clean dishes fit this exactly: the pump still circulates water, but the heater has stopped working.

## Things to try first (free)

1. Hard reset: Switch off at the wall/isolator for 10–15 minutes, then run a short program. Occasionally the fault is a one-off glitch.
2. Clean the filters: Pull out the filter assembly in the base and rinse it thoroughly. Poor water flow can sometimes upset the heating circuit.
3. Check whether it repeats: If E:09 comes back on the next cycle, it's almost certainly a hardware fault.

## Likely cause and rough costs (UK)

| Cause | Likelihood | Rough cost |
|---|---|---|
| Faulty heat pump (failed heater inside it) | Most common | Part ~£60–£150 (aftermarket at the low end, genuine Bosch higher) |
| Loose or burnt connector on the pump wiring | Occasional | Pennies if you can fix it yourself |
| Control module fault | Less common | £100–£200+ for the part |

• Engineer replacing the heat pump: typically £150–£250 all in, depending on your area and whether they use genuine parts.
• DIY: Moderately easy if you're handy. You turn off power and water, lay the machine on its back, remove the base panel, and swap the pump (a few clips and hoses). There are plenty of video guides for Bosch heat pump replacement. Expect some water spillage.

## Is it worth fixing?

A replacement SMS25AW00G-equivalent costs roughly £350–£450. So:
• Under ~6–7 years old and otherwise fine: repair is usually worth it, especially DIY.
• Older, or with other issues (leaks, rust, door problems): an engineer's bill may push you toward replacing it.

If you get an engineer out, ask them to confirm it's the heat pump before ordering parts, since that's what the bill hinges on.

I've done the power reset and it cleared the code briefly, but E:09 came back on the next cycle. The filter was already clean. The machine is 9 years old, so I'm weighing up repair against replacing it. What would you do from here?

## My recommendation

At 9 years old, I'd only repair it if you're willing to do it yourself. Otherwise I'd replace it.

## Why

• DIY repair (~£60–£120 for the part): Worth it if the machine is otherwise in good shape. Bosch dishwashers of this type often run 12–15 years, and the heat pump is one of the main wear parts. A new one could buy you several more years for a fraction of a new machine's cost.
• Engineer repair (~£150–£250): That's roughly half the price of a new machine on a 9-year-old appliance. The next fault (door springs, leaks, control board) could be close behind, and you'd have nothing to show for the repair bill. Here, replacement makes more sense.

## If you go DIY, do this first (free)

Before buying a part, confirm the diagnosis:

1. Turn off power and water, lay the machine on its back (towels down), and remove the base panel.
2. Look at the heat pump's wiring connectors. A burnt, melted, or loose plug is a known issue and might be a near-free fix.
3. If you have a multimeter, test across the heater terminals on the pump. A reading of roughly 20–40 ohms suggests the heater is fine. Open circuit (no reading) means it has failed and the pump needs replacing.

Also make sure you order the pump that matches the E-Nr and FD number on the rating plate on the door edge. Bosch used different pumps across production runs.

## Quick health check before you decide

Spend a few minutes looking for other signs of age:

• Rust or water marks under the machine
• A door that drops open heavily (worn hinge springs)
• Cracked or perished door seals
• Spray arms in poor condition

If any of those are present, I'd stop and replace it. If it's clean and solid apart from this fault, a DIY heat pump swap is a good-value fix.
I've got a multimeter but I'm not very confident around appliance wiring. If I unplug it fully and take the base panel off, is it safe to test across the heater terminals on the pump?

## Short answer: yes, it's safe if the machine is unplugged

A resistance test with a multimeter puts only a tiny battery voltage through the circuit. With the dishwasher unplugged from the wall, there's no mains power anywhere in it, so you can't get a shock from the pump terminals.

## Doing it safely

1. Pull the plug out of the socket. Don't rely on the on/off button or a wall switch. If it's hardwired to a fused spur, switch it off and remove the fuse.
2. Wait a few minutes. Then leave the control board alone. It's the only part that might briefly hold a small charge, and you don't need to touch it.
3. Manage the water. Towels down, and expect some water when you tilt it. Keep the multimeter and your hands dry.
4. Take a photo of the wiring before you unplug anything, so you can put it back exactly as it was.

## How to test

1. Unplug the connector from the heater on the pump. If you test with it still connected, you may read through other parts of the circuit. The heater usually has its own plug or two spade terminals, separate from the motor connector.
2. Set the meter to resistance (Ω), on the 200 Ω range if it isn't auto-ranging. Touch the probes together first. You should see close to 0, which confirms the meter works.
3. Probe across the two heater terminals:
• Around 20–40 Ω: the heater is fine. The fault is more likely the wiring, connector, or control module.
• Open circuit (shows "1" or "OL"): the heater has failed, so replace the pump.
4. Optional earth check: put one probe on a heater terminal and the other on a bare metal part of the pump or the earth pin. It should read open circuit. Any reading means the heater is leaking to earth, which also means replacing the pump.

While you're in there, check the connector for scorching or melted plastic.

## When to stop

If the connectors won't come off without force, or you can't work out which terminals are the heater, stop there. You've lost nothing, and you can either get an engineer to finish the diagnosis or treat it as the nudge to replace the machine.

The risky part of appliance work is having power connected. Testing with the plug out is about as safe as appliance diagnostics gets.
Thanks, that's reassuring. I unplugged it, took the base panel off and tested across the heater terminals on the pump, and the meter showed open circuit. What does that mean for repair vs replace?

## What open circuit means

The heater inside the heat pump has burnt out. That confirms the E:09 fault, and it isn't repairable on its own. You replace the whole heat pump unit.

Before ordering, check one thing: make sure the meter was set to Ω and showed close to 0 when you touched the probes together, and that you tested with the heater connector unplugged. If both are true, the result is reliable.

## Repair vs replace now

You've now confirmed the fault is the most common, most fixable one, so the case for DIY repair is strong:

| Option | Rough cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| DIY heat pump swap | £60–£150 | You've already done the hardest part (getting the machine open) |
| Engineer swap | £150–£250 | Hard to justify on a 9-year-old machine |
| New dishwasher | £350–£450 | Sensible if the machine has other wear |

My view: if your quick health check (no rust or leaks underneath, door springs OK, seals intact) came out clean, replace the pump yourself. If you spotted other problems while the base was off, put the money toward a new machine instead.

## If you go ahead

1. Order the right part. Use the E-Nr and FD number from the rating plate on the door edge. Search those with "heat pump" on a parts site or the Bosch spares site. Genuine Bosch costs more. A reputable aftermarket pump is usually fine on a machine this age.
2. Before removal: keep it unplugged, turn off the water, and photograph all wiring and hose connections.
3. The swap: disconnect the pump's electrical plugs and the hoses (expect some water), release the pump from the sump (usually a twist or clips), fit the new one, and reconnect everything exactly as in your photos.
4. Test carefully: refit the base panel loosely, restore water and power, and run a short program. Check underneath for leaks and feel whether the water gets warm. Once it's dry and heating, secure everything properly.

If any part of the removal feels beyond you once the new pump arrives, an engineer fitting a part you've supplied is usually cheaper than a full call-out with their parts.
